c1.story:
Every classification system has a drawer marked miscellaneous, and this is India's. Open it and you find a company that treats a city's sewage, a platform that books hotel rooms for travel agents, a lab that grades diamonds, a firm that runs visa counters for foreign embassies, one of the country's largest employers of security guards, a staffing giant, a state-owned e-auction house, a few makers of transformers, bimetal strips and furnace linings, a holding company and a landlord.

What do they have in common? Honestly, not much. And that is the most useful thing to know about this industry. There is no single story here, so the first job is never to ask how the sector is doing. It is to ask which door a company walks through.

Door one is the toll booth. TBO Tek, International Gemmological Institute, BLS International and MSTC each take a small cut on every booking, certificate, visa or auction that passes through them. They need almost no plant and almost no inventory. If volumes grow and nobody builds a cheaper toll gate, the profit compounds quietly.

Door two rents out people. SIS, founded in Patna by R. K. Sinha, posts guards and housekeepers at offices and factories across the country; Quess places temporary staff. The client's money mostly passes straight through to the workers' wages, and the company keeps a sliver. Scale and prompt collection are everything.

A toll booth keeps most of what it collects. A labour contractor keeps a few paise per rupee. Both are in this drawer.

Door three makes and builds things. Va Tech Wabag designs and builds water and sewage plants, including large desalination plants for Chennai. Shilchar winds transformers, Shivalik Bimetal makes the tiny shunt resistors inside smart meters, and Raghav makes the silica lining for induction furnaces. Their year depends on India's capex cycle and on what copper and steel did between the quote and the delivery.

Door four is ownership. Kama Holdings mainly owns a stake in SRF. Nirlon owns a knowledge park in Mumbai's Goregaon and collects rent from IT tenants. The question for both is simply the gap between the share price and what they own.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four completely different businesses. Read each top to bottom, and resist the temptation to compare across tiles.

  • The name and the line under it describe how the company earns: a cut on transactions, a margin on headcount, an order priced against metal, or a dividend and rent stream.
  • The tickers are the listed names behind each door. Click one for its stock page. The platform tile is the most crowded, with a travel platform, a grading lab, a visa operator and a PSU e-auction house.
  • The profit bar is the clearest signal on the card. Platforms and fees sit at the high end: little capital, little inventory, a cut on every transaction. People-heavy services sit at the low end, because the wage passes through and only a sliver stays. Projects and products sit in the middle, with the margin set by the gap between the order price and the metal price. Holding and property also sit in the middle, though the real question there is the discount to underlying value, not the margin.
  • The last line is the bet. Note how different they are: transaction volumes, headcount and collections, the capex cycle and metal, and a discount narrowing.

Below the tiles, the analogy of the toll booth, the labour contractor, the builder and the landlord gives you the four in one line.

The so-what is the rule for using everything that follows on this page: decide which door a name is behind, then judge it against that door's rules, not against its neighbours in this list. A guard company will always look terrible next to a grading lab on margins, and that comparison tells you nothing.

c2.story:
How do you draw one kitchen for a drawer this mixed? By noticing that every business here, whatever it sells, goes through the same five steps: someone originates the demand, inputs come in, the work gets done, a technology layer coordinates it, and then the company keeps earning from what it built or runs.

Station one is origination. A municipality floats a water tender. A utility orders transformers. A hotel lists rooms. An embassy outsources its visa counter. A factory hires guards. The buyers are a mix of governments, utilities, embassies, travel agents and corporates, and none of them is listed in this industry.

Station two is inputs: copper, electrical steel, aluminium, silica sand, cement, and above all people. The metals come from Hindalco and importers, the grain-oriented electrical steel inside transformers comes mostly from abroad including China, and the people come from India's vast labour market. This is where China stands as the rival in this kitchen, supplying critical steel and competing with cheap transformers and cables.

Station three is build and deliver. This is the busiest station: Wabag building treatment plants, Shilchar and V-Marc winding transformers and drawing cables, Shivalik and Raghav making components and refractories, SIS and Quess posting staff, IGI grading stones.

A metal shock hits the builder within a quarter. A wage revision hits the guard company at once. Neither touches the toll booth.

Station four is the technology layer. Software matches a travel agent to a hotel room, tracks guards on duty, runs MSTC's e-auctions of scrap and minerals, and manages the visa queue. TBO Tek, MSTC and BLS stand here, against global rivals such as the big online travel platforms and, in grading, GIA.

Station five is operations and annuity. Wabag runs the plants it builds for years under operations contracts. SIS renews its security contracts. Nirlon collects rent and Kama collects dividends. This is the recurring income that steadies the lumpier stations.

The reason the doors rarely move together is visible right here: each shock enters at a different station.
c2.read:
Five boxes across the top, a band row underneath. Read the boxes left to right.

The five boxes run from origination on the left to operations and annuity on the right. Under each name you get what happens there and who stands there. Notice how the who lines switch from buyers at station one, to metal makers and the labour market at station two, to the listed names from station three onward.

The band row tells the story. Station one is government and corporates, the customers. Station two is coloured as the rival band, metal and Chinese steel: the input this industry cannot control and partly imports from its competitor. Then listed India holds the last three stations in a row: build and deliver, the technology layer and operations. Unlike many industries, listed companies here own the whole back half of the chain, including the recurring-income end.

Then read the geography note. The product makers cluster in the engineering belts of Gujarat, Pune and Rajasthan and compete with Chinese transformer and cable exporters on price. The service names are everywhere India has an office, embassy or factory gate, and their real competitor is the unorganised sector paying lower wages.

Use the diagram as a shock map, which is exactly what the so-what line beneath does. Trace a copper spike from station two to the project and product names at station three: it hits within a quarter. Trace a minimum-wage revision, also a station-two input, to the guard and staffing names: immediate. Then trace either one to the platforms at station four. Nothing arrives. That is why the four doors behave like four different industries.

c3.story:
If this industry has no single story, it also has no single customer. Each door borrows its demand from a completely different buyer, and the best way to forecast any name here is to read that buyer's budget rather than the company's own commentary.

Take the water companies. Their customers are state and municipal water utilities, funded by central water missions, state budgets and loans from the World Bank and the Japanese aid agency. When a mission is announced, tenders follow for years. When a state's finances are stretched, payments slow. Wabag's fortunes therefore track Delhi's and the states' water priorities more than anything happening in the market.

The transformer, cable and component makers sell to power utilities and renewable developers. Here the driver is transmission capex, the solar and wind build-out, and the smart-meter rollout, which needs a tiny shunt resistor in every meter. When Power Grid and the state transmission companies are ordering, these makers are busy.

The travel platform and the visa operator ride a completely different wave: outbound and domestic travel, visa rules, airfares. Covid took both to almost nothing in 2020; reopening brought them roaring back.

Read the buyer's budget, not this industry's headlines. Each door is borrowing someone else's demand.

The diamond grader depends on the trade in Surat, where most of the world's diamonds are cut and polished, and on American jewellery demand. Lab-grown stones have been a mixed blessing: more stones need certificates, but lab-grown prices collapsed through 2024 and 2025, and the fee per stone came under pressure.

Security and staffing follow office occupancy, hiring cycles and minimum wages. Refractories and e-auctions follow steel output and scrap prices. And the landlord follows IT hiring, the return to office and Mumbai rents.

Eight customer groups, eight different cycles. That diversity is what makes the industry confusing at the sector level, and very readable at the company level.
c3.read:
Eight tiles, one per customer group. Each has three lines.

  • The name is who is buying.
  • What it buys tells you which door benefits. Water plants and operations contracts point to Wabag. Transformers, cables and shunts point to the product makers. Room inventory and booking engines point to the travel platform. Visa counters to BLS. Grading certificates to IGI. Guards and contract staff to SIS and Quess. Ramming mass and scrap auctions to Raghav and MSTC. Office space to Nirlon.
  • What moves it is your watch list, and every tile has a different one: water missions, transmission capex, travel and visa rules, tender renewals, Surat volumes, office occupancy, steel output, IT hiring.

This grid is unusual because almost every tile maps to a single company or two. In most industries, several companies share each customer. Here, a company is essentially one tile. So the grid works less as a sector map and more as a lookup table: find your company's tile and read its moves-with line.

A useful exercise is to sort the tiles into government-paid and privately paid. Water utilities, power utilities, foreign governments and, through MSTC, parts of the steel trade are government-linked: big orders, slower payments. Travel agents, the diamond trade, corporates and IT tenants pay faster and are more cyclical in volume.

The so-what under the grid gives the operating rule: read the buyer's budget, not this industry's headlines, to know what next quarter looks like.

c4.story:
Imagine four shops on one street. The toll booth keeps most of what it collects. The labour contractor keeps a few paise per rupee. The builder's year depends on what copper did between the quote and the delivery. The landlord just needs the tenant to stay. That is this industry's P&L in a sentence, and the two charts on this card draw the extremes.

Start with the platform. A travel platform or grading lab has almost no raw-material bill. What it spends is on people and technology: engineers to run the booking engine, gemmologists to grade stones, sales teams to sign up agents and jewellers. That spend is largely fixed. So when volumes grow, revenue rises much faster than cost, and margins widen. This is operating leverage, the reason investors pay high multiples for platforms.

The project and product maker is the mirror image. Copper, steel and other materials take most of every rupee of sales. People and overheads are a modest slice. The margin is the thin gap between the order price and the input cost, and since many orders are quoted at fixed prices, a copper spike between quote and delivery comes straight out of that gap.

For a platform, growth widens the margin. For a builder, metal decides it.

The guard and staffing companies have their own peculiar shape. Their input is wages, which they pass through to clients, but with a lag. When a state raises minimum wages mid-contract, the company pays the higher wage at once and recovers it only when the contract reprices. Employee cost is the line to watch.

Working capital is where the government-facing names suffer. Water boards and power utilities pay months late, so receivable days are the honest measure of a project company's health. And for the holding company, the P&L is almost entirely other income: Kama's dividend from SRF is the business.

Four shops, four P&Ls. Reading this industry means switching lenses for every name.
c4.read:
Two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of sales down to what is left: platforms and fees on the left, projects and products on the right. They are about as different as two charts on this page can be.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar, materials or pass-through wages, is a sliver for the platform, about a tenth. For the project maker it swallows about two thirds.
  • The opex bar, people, rent and technology, flips the picture. For the platform it is the biggest bar by far, over half of sales. For the project maker it is about a sixth.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is small in both, a little bigger for the platform's technology.
  • The last bar is what is left. The platform keeps nearly three tenths; the project maker about a tenth.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the amount.

The point to take away: the platform's big cost is mostly fixed, so extra volume falls largely to profit. The project maker's big cost moves with every order and every copper tick.

The list below marks which lines matter. Gross margin or take rate, employee cost, working capital and other income all get a yes, each for a different door. Depreciation, capex and interest get a sometimes. Tax gets a no.

The so-what tells you which lens to use: platforms on take rate and volume, services on employee cost and receivables, projects on order book and gross margin, and holding companies on the discount to what they own.

c5.story:
Ask whether this industry is cyclical and the honest answer is: partly, in four different ways, plus one that overrides all of them.

The project and product makers ride India's capex cycle and the metal price. The travel and visa names ride the travel cycle. Guards and staffing barely cycle at all, since offices need security in good years and bad. But all of these companies are small caps, and small caps ride the smallcap liquidity cycle hardest of all. When money floods into smallcap funds, every name here gets re-rated regardless of merit. When it drains out, they fall together.

The last full cycle shows it clearly. In 2016 and 2017, smallcap money poured in, engineering order books swelled and many mid-sized industrial names doubled. The smallcap index peaked in January 2018. Then IL&FS, a big infrastructure lender, collapsed later that year, freezing infrastructure finance and slowing state payments. Project companies bled on receivables. And in 2020 Covid finished the job: travel and visa volumes went to almost zero, sites shut and many of these stocks traded at a fraction of book value.

In this drawer, the stock cycle is wilder than the business cycle. Liquidity sets the tide; the business only decides who swims.

The recovery came in layers. Reopening in 2021 and 2022 brought travel roaring back and the smart-meter rollout began. In 2023 and 2024, a global transformer shortage let Indian makers export at fat margins, and the IPO window opened: TBO Tek listed in May 2024 and IGI in December 2024. Smallcap multiples climbed to levels last seen in 2018.

Then 2025 tested everything at once: a sharp smallcap correction early in the year, steep US tariffs on Indian goods in August, and the collapse in lab-grown diamond prices. Transformer prices stopped rising.

By 2026 the product names have revived, helped by the GST overhaul and shifts in Chinese exports, and order books are full. But valuations are rich again, and the smallcap index has climbed a long way. The risk is no longer a demand hole. It is a metal spike or a liquidity turn.
c5.read:
Three parts: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years under each belong to the last cycle, and it was short and sharp: boom in 2016 and 2017, peak in 2018, bust from 2018 to 2020, bottom in 2020. The arrow sits in the boom arc, labelled capex-led boom: order books full, multiples stretched. Hover an arc for what defined it.

The timeline from 2019 is colour-coded. Two bust years, the IL&FS hangover and Covid. A neutral 2021 to 2022 for the reopening. Boom for 2023 to 2024, the transformer shortage and the IPO window. Neutral for 2025, the smallcap correction, tariffs and lab-grown collapse. And the now entry for 2026.

The four hands each speak for a different door.

  • Transmission and utility capex tenders: strong, arrow up. The product door's order books keep filling.
  • Copper and electrical steel prices: rising, arrow down. This hurts fixed-price orders until they reprice.
  • Outbound travel and visa volumes: growing, arrow up. Good for the platforms.
  • Smallcap index breadth: frothy, a mixed reading. Narrowing breadth after a long rally is how these names fall by half.

Two hands up, one down, one mixed. The down arrow and the mixed one are the two risks the so-what line names: a metal spike and a liquidity turn. Demand is fine. Price, both of copper and of the stocks, is the question.

c6.story:
With four doors and a dozen businesses, you might expect a dashboard of forty dials. In practice a handful do most of the work, and two of them dominate.

The first is government capex on water and power. Tenders for treatment plants, transformers and cables fill project order books for years, and the transmission plan that India needs to connect its solar and wind farms is the single biggest source of that capex. The second is copper, the main input for cables, transformers and bimetal strips. It is a diamond, not a simple red arrow. A copper spike squeezes margins on fixed-price orders, but it also lifts the value of inventory already bought at lower prices, so a company can report a pleasant quarter just before an unpleasant one.

Transmission tenders decide how much work there is. Copper decides how much of it is profitable.

Then a ring of two-dot dials. Capital goods output lifts every industrial door at once: more factories need more furnaces, more refractories and more guards at the gate. Interest rates hit twice, through project finance and working capital costs, and through smallcap liquidity. The rupee is two-faced: a weaker rupee helps transformer exporters but makes outbound travel dearer. US tariffs, which rose steeply on Indian goods in 2025, threaten the export window that transformer makers enjoyed during the global shortage. Minimum wage revisions squeeze guard and staffing margins until contracts reprice.

And one more two-dot dial matters more than its weight suggests: smallcap liquidity itself. Flows into smallcap funds re-rate every name here regardless of merit, and they are tracked here through the broad market as a stand-in.

Finally, two one-dot dials for single companies. Steel output drives induction-furnace utilisation, and so demand for Raghav's ramming mass and MSTC's scrap auctions. Lab-grown diamond prices drive the value of each certificate IGI issues. Small dials, but for those companies, they are the whole dashboard.
c6.read:
One row per dial. Read across: the dial, its channel, what a rise does, the weight and today's reading.

  • Channel: the route into profits. In this industry the channel column also tells you which door a dial belongs to. Tenders for plants and cables: projects. Wage bills: services. Transformer exports and outbound travel, on one row: both products and platforms.
  • A rise does: five green up arrows, for government capex, capital goods output, steel output, lab-grown prices and smallcap liquidity. Three red down arrows, for interest rates, US tariffs and minimum wages. Two diamonds, for copper and the rupee.
  • Weight: two rows carry three dots, government capex on water and power, and copper. Six carry two.

The last column shows today's reading where a dial maps to a series we track: the infrastructure index for capex, copper, capital goods output, the money-market rate, the rupee, consumer inflation as a stand-in for wage pressure, steel output, and the broad market for liquidity. US tariffs and lab-grown prices show a dash; you read those from the news.

How to use it: start with the two three-dot rows, which together set the margin of the biggest door, the product makers. Then pick out the dials for your specific company. A guard company owner should watch the wage row. A travel platform owner the rupee. A grading lab owner the lab-grown row. Because the doors are so different, most investors here need only three or four of these rows.

The so-what line repeats the headline: track transmission capex tenders and the copper price.

c7.story:
Every business in this drawer has a different bottleneck, but three of them are permanent, and they quietly cap returns no matter how good the cycle looks.

The first is government payment delays. Municipal and state utility customers pay months late. A water company can show a profit on paper and still be starved of cash, borrowing to fund the gap while it waits. This is the oldest problem in Indian project businesses, and it surfaced again when state payments slowed after the IL&FS collapse.

The second is electrical steel. The grain-oriented steel inside every transformer is mostly imported. A supply squeeze abroad or a change in duty lands straight on a transformer maker's margin, and there is little it can do in the short run.

The third is the holding-company discount. Kama Holdings trades well below the value of its SRF stake, and like most Indian holding companies, the gap rarely closes on its own. Buying it for the discount is a bet that something, a restructuring, a buyback, a change in sentiment, will close it.

A holding company's discount is the one bottleneck that is both permanent and, occasionally, the whole opportunity.

Then the recurring risks. Guard and staffing contracts reprice yearly, so a mid-year minimum wage hike is absorbed first and recovered later. And tender concentration haunts the visa and water names: when one embassy or one state re-tenders, a company can lose a big slice of its business overnight.

Two cyclical bottlenecks are worth watching closely. Every transformer and cable maker is adding lines at once to meet the shortage. When they all finish, pricing will normalise, and the fat margins of 2023 and 2024 will look like the peak they were. And smallcap liquidity is thin: a few redemptions can move prices by a fifth, making the stock cycle wilder than the business cycle.

Finally, a slow one: lab-grown diamonds. Cheaper stones still need grading, but at lower fees and with rival labs competing on price.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, with why it bites and a severity label. The label tells you how to treat it.

  • Structural: government payment delays, electrical steel import dependence and the holding-company discount. These are permanent. Price them into what you are willing to pay rather than waiting for them to disappear.
  • Recurring: wage pass-through lag and tender concentration. These return regularly and make individual quarters or individual years jumpy, especially for the services and visa names.
  • Cyclical: capacity additions chasing a shortage, and smallcap liquidity. Both are favourable right now and both will turn. The first decides when transformer margins peak; the second decides when the stocks fall together.
  • Slow: lab-grown disruption, a gradual pressure on grading fees.

Notice that each row tends to belong to one door. Payment delays and tender concentration: projects and visa. Electrical steel and capacity additions: products. Wage lag: services. Holding discount: the holding door. Lab-grown: the grading lab. Only smallcap liquidity cuts across all of them. That is the bottleneck table version of this industry's central lesson: four doors, four different sets of risks.

The so-what line under the table says the first two rows cap returns on the biggest door for good, and the next three are headline risks worth a per-company news alert. In practice: set an alert for minimum wage notifications if you own a services name, for tender renewals if you own a visa or water name, and for any discount-closing corporate action if you own the holding company.

c8.story:
When each company in a sector has a different customer, each also has a different regulator. So this rulebook reads less like one industry's rules and more like a directory of who can change each company's year with a single notification.

For the water companies, it is the Ministry of Jal Shakti and the pollution boards. A new water mission becomes a multi-year tender pipeline. A tightened discharge norm becomes a retrofit order, since every plant that no longer meets the standard must be upgraded.

For the transformer and component makers, it is the Ministry of Power and the Central Electricity Authority. The national transmission plan is essentially the product door's order book, smart-meter mandates drive demand for meter components, and efficiency standards for transformers can force replacements. Alongside them, BIS quality control orders require imported cables, transformers and steel to meet Indian standards, which in practice works like a tariff against Chinese imports.

For a visa company, one tender renewal is the whole business. For a guard company, one wage notification is the whole margin.

For the visa operator, the regulator is a mix of India's Ministry of External Affairs and the foreign governments whose counters it runs. A single tender renewal can make or break years of revenue.

For the guard companies, the Private Security Agencies Regulation Act licenses operators state by state. That raises the bar for the unorganised sector, which is the guards' real competition. And the Code on Wages, together with state minimum wages, sets the floor under every guard's and contract worker's pay. Each revision is a margin event until contracts reprice.

Trade rules matter for the exporters. DGFT sets export incentives and import duties on steel and copper, and US tariff authorities, after the steep 2025 tariffs on Indian goods, are the biggest external risk to the transformer export story.

Finally, SEBI and the stock exchanges. It sounds odd to list the market regulator as an industry rule, but in this drawer of small caps, half the headlines are splits, bonuses, SME listings and promoter sales rather than business news.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care and its status.

  • Always: four rows. The Ministry of Jal Shakti with the pollution boards, the Ministry of External Affairs and foreign governments, the Private Security Agencies Regulation Act, and SEBI with the exchanges. These are permanent and each belongs to one door: water, visa, guards and every small cap.
  • Live: four rows. The Ministry of Power with the CEA, BIS quality control orders, the Code on Wages with state minimum wages, and DGFT trade rules. These are actively shaping orders, margins and competitiveness right now.
  • New: one row, US tariff authorities. It is the newest and arguably the largest external risk, aimed squarely at the transformer and refractory exporters.

The trick with this table is to find your company's row first and ignore the rest. Owning Wabag? The Jal Shakti row. SIS or Quess? The security act and the wage code. BLS? External Affairs. A transformer maker? Power, BIS, DGFT and the US tariff row together, the most crowded set of rules for any door here.

Then read the SEBI row with a sceptical eye. Corporate actions such as splits and bonus issues change the number of shares, not the value of the business. In a drawer full of small caps, separating corporate-action noise from business news is half the job.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces ask who keeps the money. Run this drawer through the test and it splits cleanly in two: the platforms keep a lot, and the project and service businesses keep very little.

Start with rivalry. A grading lab or a travel platform typically faces one or two serious rivals. IGI's main competitor in grading is GIA; TBO Tek competes with a few global distribution platforms. A cable maker or a guard company, by contrast, competes with hundreds of organised rivals and thousands of unorganised ones. Price wars are a fact of life there.

Suppliers tell the same story. Platforms buy software and people, neither of which can squeeze them much. Product makers buy copper and steel from sellers with real pricing power, often at world prices.

Fragmented buyers, few rivals: that is a toll booth. Powerful buyers, many rivals: that is a job.

The buyer column is the most decisive. A travel platform's customers are thousands of small travel agents; a grading lab's are thousands of jewellers and diamond traders. None of them, individually, can dictate terms. The project and service companies face the opposite: governments and utilities that set the terms, the penalties and the payment dates, and pay late.

Entry is somewhat harder for platforms, protected by trust and network effects: a jeweller wants a certificate buyers recognise, and an agent wants the platform every hotel is on. Capital and licences give the product names only a little protection.

But here is the twist. On substitutes, the platforms are more exposed. Hotels push direct booking to avoid paying a platform's cut, and large diamond houses could grade in-house. Nothing replaces a transformer or a guard at the gate.

The net result is the profit bar from the first card. The platforms keep most of the profit because their buyers are fragmented and their rivals few. The project and services doors give most of it away to the metal seller, the utility and the wage board.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes: platforms and fees, and projects and services combined. Look at size first. The projects shape is much larger, touching the outer ring on rivalry and buyer power and close to it on suppliers. The platforms shape is compact, pulled in on suppliers especially.

Now find the crossing. On substitutes, the platform reaches further, two against one and a half. That is the direct-booking and in-house grading threat from the story. It is the one place where the toll booth is more exposed than the builder.

The table beside it gives every score from zero to three with a reason.

  • Rivalry: one and a half against three. One or two rivals versus hundreds.
  • Supplier: one against two and a half. Software and people versus copper and steel sellers. The widest gap on the chart.
  • Buyer: one and a half against three. Fragmented agents and jewellers versus governments that pay late.
  • Entrants: one and a half against two. Network effects help the platforms a little more than licences help the builders.
  • Substitutes: two against one and a half.

Remember that the second shape blends two doors, projects and people-heavy services. If you own a guard company, mentally push the supplier spoke toward labour pressure; if you own a transformer maker, push it toward metal. And if you own a platform, keep an eye on the substitutes spoke: it is the one most likely to grow.

c10.story:
With four doors, you might think you need four cheat sheets. Instead, this one uses eight numbers that work across doors, with a different good mark for each. Read them right and they will even tell you which door a company is really behind.

For the project names, start with order book to sales: how many years of work are already in hand. A falling book-to-bill, new orders lagging revenue, is the first warning. Then gross margin or take rate: for a product maker, it is the gap between order price and metal; for a platform, the cut per transaction. A transformer maker earning an unusually fat gross margin is living through a shortage, which is lovely while it lasts.

For the services names, the key is employee cost to sales. Flat quarter on quarter means wage hikes are being passed through. A jump without a matching revenue jump means the company is absorbing a wage revision, at least for now.

EBITDA margin is the door detector. Platforms, products and services each live in a different band.

Receivable days apply to everyone but bite hardest for water and power project names, whose customers are governments. Then EBITDA margin, which the cheat sheet itself says tells you the door the company is really behind: platforms earn far higher margins than product makers, which earn far more than guard and staffing firms. If a company's margin does not match its claimed door, ask why.

Return on capital tells you whether growth earns its keep, with each door having its own good mark. Capex to depreciation tells you whether the product names are adding lines into the shortage, and warns you if they are still building as prices soften. And sales growth tells you whether the volume story is intact, again with a different bar for platforms, products and services.
c10.read:
One row per number. Read across: the metric, what it tells you, what good looks like and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you: the question to ask of each company.
  • What good looks like: the only column with figures, and in this industry almost every row gives separate benchmarks for platforms, products and services. Find your company's door first, then read only its benchmark. A guard company should never be judged against a platform's return on capital.
  • Today's industry median: from the latest annual filings in our database. Only order book to sales lacks a median, because it comes from presentations.

Here the median needs extra care. It blends a travel platform, a guard company, a water builder, a transformer maker and a holding company. It is a statistical average of businesses that have nothing in common, so it tells you little about any one of them. Use it, at most, as a rough sense of whether small industrial names as a group are having a good year.

The more powerful use of the table is the EBITDA margin row as a door detector. Compare a company's margin with the three bands. If a so-called platform earns a services-like margin, or a product maker earns a platform-like margin, find out why before you trust either label.

A good reading order: for products, gross margin, then order book, then capex to depreciation. For services, employee cost, then receivables. For platforms, sales growth, then take rate. For the holding company, none of these: compare the market value with the value of what it owns.

c11.story:
Because each door in this drawer runs on its own clock, the outside signals that warn you are spread across a wide range of lead times. The trick is to know which signal belongs to which company.

The earliest warning, three quarters ahead, is the central water mission's budget allocation. Money budgeted today becomes tenders, then orders, then revenue for the water builders most of a year later.

Two quarters ahead come Power Grid and state transmission company tender awards. Today's award is the transformer and cable order executed two quarters on. That is the single most important signal for the product door, and it is why the call keeps returning to transmission.

One quarter ahead you have copper and electrical steel prices, which hit next quarter's margin on fixed-price orders. Surat polishing volumes and lab-grown prices, since stones are cut first and graded a quarter later. State minimum wage notifications, since wages rise at once and contracts reprice later. Steel production and scrap prices, which set refractory and e-auction volumes.

And in the same quarter: outbound passenger numbers and visa issuance, which turn straight into bookings and fees, and smallcap fund flows, which move these share prices before any earnings move.

Transmission tenders tell you about next year's work. Smallcap flows tell you about next week's price.

The three-sign rule here applies only to the product door, the biggest one. It is in a real up-cycle when utility tenders are rising, gross margins are holding against metal, and receivable days are flat or falling. Two of three means a healthy boom; one of three a stretched one. Today: tenders rising, a tick; receivables mostly stable, a tick; margins holding against metal, a cross, because copper is up while prices are flat.

So the call: mid-boom and priced for it. Prefer platforms with growing volumes and project names with flat receivables, and avoid paying boom multiples for a cable or transformer maker whose margin is already past its best.

The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for its channel.

For this industry the dots are spread from end to end. Two sit at the far left, same quarter: outbound passengers and visa issuance, and smallcap fund flows. Four sit at one quarter: copper and electrical steel, Surat volumes with lab-grown prices, state minimum wage notifications, and steel production with scrap prices. One sits at two quarters: transmission tender awards. And one sits furthest right, at three quarters: the central water mission's budget allocations.

Because each dot belongs to a particular door, use the chart as a door-by-door reading order rather than a single sequence. Products: transmission awards, then copper. Water: mission budgets, then state payments. Services: wage notifications. Platforms: travel and visa data, then Surat volumes for the grading lab. Everyone: smallcap flows.

Below the chart is the rule for the product door, with its three signs.

  • Utility tenders rising: a tick, transmission plan intact.
  • Gross margins holding against metal: a cross, copper up and prices flat.
  • Receivable days flat or falling: a tick, mostly stable.

Two of three: a healthy boom by the rule's own definition, but with margin under pressure.

Finally, the call box with its points and what would change it. Keep the last three as alerts: a sustained copper and electrical steel spike without order repricing, a smallcap liquidity reversal like early 2025, and, on the upside, US tariff relief or Chinese export curbs that widen the export window.
